draft.title: The remainder and factor theorems
card: When a polynomial \(P(x)\) is divided by \(x - a\), the remainder is \(P(a)\). This is the value you get by putting \(x = a\) into \(P(x)\).
Find the remainder when \(P(x) = x^{3} + 2x - 5\) is divided by \(x - 2\). Here \(a = 2\), so \(P(2) = 8 + 4 - 5 = 7\). The remainder is 7.
If \(P(a) = 0\), the remainder is zero, so \(x - a\) is a factor of \(P(x)\). If \(P(a) \ne 0\), then \(x - a\) is not a factor.
To factorise, test small whole numbers such as \(\pm 1\) and \(\pm 2\) until \(P(a) = 0\). Then \(x - a\) is a factor, and a root of \(P(x) = 0\) is \(x = a\).
draft.remember: Put \(x = a\) in to get the remainder. A remainder of zero means \(x - a\) is a factor.

a.q: What is the remainder when \(P(x) = x^{3} - 4x + 3\) is divided by \(x - 3\)?
a.why: Here \(a = 3\), so \(P(3) = 27 - 12 + 3 = 18\). Using \(-3\) instead gives \(-27 + 12 + 3 = -12\), which is the sign mistake of using the wrong value for \(a\).

b.q: Which of these is a factor of \(P(x) = x^{3} - 7x + 6\)?
b.why: \(P(1) = 1 - 7 + 6 = 0\), so \(x - 1\) is a factor. The tempting \(x + 1\) needs \(P(-1) = 0\), but \(P(-1) = -1 + 7 + 6 = 12\). Also \(P(3) = 12\) and \(P(-2) = 12\), so the other two are not factors.
b.clue: A factor \(x - a\) needs \(P(a) = 0\), so test each value of \(a\).

check.summary: No problems found. Both answers check out: P(3) = 18 in (a), and only x - 1 is a factor in (b), since P(1) = 0 and P(3), P(-1) and P(-2) all equal 12.
